It solves the problem of diverging viewing rays in perspective projection, which prevents the uniform sampling rates required for efficient fixed-weight interpolation [S1, unofficial][S2].

The claim states that the evidence supports the idea that the method solves the problem of diverging viewing rays in perspective projection, thereby preventing the need for uniform sampling rates required for efficient fixed-weight interpolation. Source [S1] explicitly notes that 'Perspective rays diverge, so uniform sampling is hard' and describes the shear-warp algorithm's use of 'adaptive area sampling' where 'each slice is scaled differently'. Source [S2] confirms that the shear-warp factorization provides a 'simple and efficient solution to the sampling problem for perspective projections' by ensuring that 'within each slice the sampling rate is uniform... so there is no need to implement a complicated multirate filter.' This aligns with the claim that the method addresses the diverging ray issue to avoid complex/uniform sampling requirements across the entire volume.

It is more computationally expensive than parallel Shear-warp due to the additional resampling and complex control flow, but remains significantly faster than general ray-casting for large datasets [S2, S4].

The claim states that the algorithm is more computationally expensive than parallel Shear-warp due to additional resampling and complex control flow. Source [S2] explicitly states: 'The perspective algorithm is more expensive than the parallel projection algorithm because extra time is required to compute resampling weights and because the many-to-one mapping from voxels to pixels complicates the flow of control.' Source [S4] also supports the cost aspect, noting: 'the scaled shear-warp is slower than the parallel shear-warp because of the additional resampling of the volume data.' Regarding the second part of the claim, that it remains significantly faster than general ray-casting for large datasets, Source [S4] highlights the efficiency of the shear-warp factorization compared to pixel-order (ray-casting) renderers, noting that ray-casters are inefficient for distributed data and that the shear-warp approach allows rendering of large datasets (>1GB) efficiently on clusters, whereas ray-casting would require all nodes to access all data. Thus, the evidence supports all parts of the claim.
supported
Previous parallel S-W implementations (VolPack, volsh, Virvo) require all nodes to know all data, limiting them to volumes fitting in a single node's memory [S4].

The claim is explicitly stated in the provided text. In the 'Introduction' section of Source [S4], it says: 'A few parallel implementations of the S-W factorisation already exist (e.g. VolPack [Lacroute & Levoy 1994]; the National Center for Atmospheric Research’s volsh; Virvo [Schulze & Lang 2002]), but none distribute the data — all nodes “know” all of the data. In practice this limits these systems to rendering data volumes which, in their entirety, fit in a single node’s memory space.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
The scale factor ensures the slice closest to the viewer is scaled by 1.0, and no slice is enlarged [S2].

The claim states that the scale factor ensures the slice closest to the viewer is scaled by 1.0 and no slice is enlarged. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly states: 'We always choose a factorization of the viewing transformation in which the slice closest to the viewer is scaled by a factor of one so that no slice is ever! enlarged.' This directly supports every part of the claim.
